# 

Greeting Machine is an abstract robotic object engineered to initiate social interactions by engaging passersby and catalyzing opening encounters.

### What is it?

In our work on the Greeting Machine, we set out to redefine robotic interactions by designing an abstract object that sparks spontaneous, human-centered encounters. Rather than adhering to conventional roles, the machine invites playful engagement, prompting users to connect in ways that blur the traditional boundaries between art and technology. Presented at RO-MAN 2018, this project reflects our belief that thoughtful design can transform routine interactions into meaningful experiences, challenging expectations and opening up new avenues for communication in everyday settings.

︎ milab.idc.ac.il

An abstract robotic object, capable of social encounters
Image
The Greeting Machine is a robotic object, designed to convey the social interaction of greeting using only a minimalistic movement, while bearing no resemblance to humans, animals, household objects or most familiar robots. 
To create expressive movement, gestures were designed with movement experts such as a choreographer, puppeteer and animator.
Experiments with the Greeting Machine show that it not only creates an experience perceived as an opening encounter, but, through the gesture design, it can also evoke positive and negative experiences. This indicates that an abstract, simple object, with very limited motion can create a social interaction experience through gesture design.

## IN A NUTSHELL

We think about smart/learning objects as yet not finished entities that can evolve their behaviors by observing, reading and interpreting our habits. They train their algorithms based on deep learning or similar ways to constantly adapt and refine their decisions.
But What if things are not that good at learning after all without some help?
What if in a near future, i could just get a person to train my products better as i do with pets?
Why having to deal with the initial problems and risk that it might even learn wrongly?
So, What if there would be an algorithm trainer?

Lucy Anderson-Bashan¹ Benny Megidish¹ Hadas Erel¹

<Abstract—> Opening encounters are an integral element of everyday social interaction, and are essential for forming and maintaining social relationships between people. We present an abstract non-humanoid robotic object called the Greeting Machine, designed to communicate positive and negative social cues in the context of opening encounters. The design includes a small ball rolling on a larger dome, with a custom gear and lever mechanism that supports a variety of subtle movements. Gestures were designed with movement experts, and were evaluated using a physical first-person qualitative study. Our findings reveal that an abstract robot designed with no specific metaphor can effectively take part in opening encounters. Furthermore, a minimal brief movement, designed as an Approach or Avoid gesture, may be enough to evoke positive and negative experiences. Most of them also include verbal greetings [12]. Human Robot Interaction (HRI) researchers studied a variety of opening encounters with humanoid robots. Behaviors were usually human-like and included communication cues such as facial expressions, nodding, hand-waving, and eye gaze [13]–[15]. These human-like non-verbal behaviors were shown to be successfully interpreted as social cues [13], [16]. A few studies tested social interactions including opening encounters with non-humanoid robots designed as everyday devices, such as an ottoman, a car seat, and automatic doors [17]–[19]. The non verbal cues expressed by these non-humanoid robots were successfully interpreted as a social interaction related to greeting.

Oren Zuckerman, miLAB Director: Greeting is such an important social feature, we hoped that our research will show that social objects like the Greeting Machine may improve well-being, by adding short, positive social-encounters to everyday life.

Iddo Wald, miLAB Faculty: We decided to study if minimal gestures can create meaningful social interactions. We strive to define the "body language" of robotic objects, and create guidelines that will hopefully empower robot designers when working on social gestures. Minimal gestures can lead to low-cost and low-complexity robots. Minimal gestures can also be added to IoT devices and home assistants, adding the "social" aspects to existing smart objects.

Image: IDC Herzliya

It sounds like the specific design of the Greeting Machine is based on a variety of research. Can you describe how you decided on the shapes and motions that comprise the robot?

Benny Megidish, miLAB Student: We wanted to avoid immediate associations to humans or creatures, so we created a variety of low-fidelity shapes inspired by Gestalt psychology (cone, pyramid, sphere). We decided to design it as a sphere due to its symmetry around all axis, and also because curvilinear shapes are considered to be symbols of warmth and happiness. We were also greatly inspired by character animation, and added the small ball according to generate expressive movement. The result was a unique language formed by the relationship between the two spherical forms. From a technical perspective, we leveraged the geometrical properties of the large sphere to create random secondary motion of the small ball. The combination of professionally animated movement and random secondary motion lead to fluent natural movement.

L29@P1: Birthe Nesset1, Marta Romeo1, Gnanathusharan Rajendran2and Helen Hastie1
L30@P1: Abstract— Trust repair strategies are an important part of
L31@P1: human-robot interaction. In this study, we investigate how
L32@P1: repeated failures impact users’ trust and how we might mitigate
L33@P1: them. Specifically, we look at different repair strategies in the
L34@P1: form of apologies, with additional features to them such as
L35@P1: warnings and promises. Through an online study, we explore
L36@P1: these repair strategies for repeated failures in the form of
L37@P1: robot incongruence, where there is a mismatch of verbal and
L38@P1: non-verbal information given by the robot. Our results show
L39@P1: that such incongruent robot behaviour has a significant overall
L40@P1: negative impact on participants’ trust. We found that the robot
L41@P1: making a promise, and then breaking it, results in a significant
L42@P1: decrease in participants’ trust, when compared to a general
L43@P1: apology as a repair strategy. These findings contribute to the
L44@P1: research on trust repair strategies and, additionally, shed light
L45@P1: on how robot failures, in the form of incongruences, impact
L46@P1: participants’ trust.
L47@P1: I. INTRODUCTION
L48@P1: With the growing development of social robots, various
L49@P1: robot failures need to be mitigated for. With social robots,
L50@P1: not only should one handle technical shortcomings and errors
L51@P1: from the robot, but a whole new spectrum of interaction
L52@P1: failures need to be taken into consideration as well. The robot
L53@P1: might say or do something unexpected or uncalled for, which
L54@P1: breaks with the users’ understanding of the interaction or
L55@P1: their perception of the robot’s abilities [1], [2].
L56@P1: When this happens, different trust repair strategies could
L57@P1: be implemented to mitigate some of the loss of trust [3].
L58@P1: Usually, the robot will apologise for committing a failure,
L59@P1: often using additional tools such as emotions or promises
L60@P1: [4], [3], [5]. Apologies seem to work well in single-failure
L61@P1: situations. However, once a failure has happened, this does
L62@P1: not necessarily mean that the interaction stops nor that
L63@P1: additional failures will not happen. In fact, if the failure does
L64@P1: not have any severe or harmful consequences, users might
L65@P1: continue with the interaction, thus potentially causing the
L66@P1: same failure to repeat itself [6].
L67@P1: An example of unexpected mannerisms is a robot’s incongruence. The robot might respond to a user with emotions
L68@P1: or facial expressions that do not fit the conversation, or it
L69@P1: might behave in an unanticipated manner, such as turning at
L70@P1: unexpected times or answering a question while addressing
L71@P1: the incorrect person [7], [8]. These incongruencies, though
L72@P1: not always wrong nor harmful, could be perceived as a robot
L73@P1: This work was funded and supported by the UKRI Node on Trust
L74@P1: (EP/V026682/1) https://trust.tas.ac.uk
L75@P1: 1School of Mathematical and Computer Sciences, Heriot-Watt
L76@P1: University, UK. bn25@hw.ac.uk, m.romeo@he.ac.uk,
L77@P1: h.hastie@hw.ac.uk 2School of Social Sciences, Heriot-Watt
L78@P1: University, UK. t.rajendran@hw.ac.uk
L79@P1: failure by the user, causing potential decreases in trust and
L80@P1: negatively impacting the users’ attitude towards the robot’s
L81@P1: capabilities [9]. In this paper, we aim to expand on the
L82@P1: current literature on repair strategies in the form of apologies,
L83@P1: by adding extra features to them such as warnings and
L84@P1: promises, in interactions with a repeated failure in the form
L85@P1: of a robot incongruence between the robot’s gestures and its
L86@P1: verbal command.
L87@P1: This study can be divided into two main research questions. In the first part, we look at how introducing a robot
L88@P1: failure might impact users’ trust. With this in mind, we
L89@P1: propose the following hypothesis: H1: A robot failure will
L90@P1: significantly reduce users’ trust.
L91@P1: The second part of the study looks at the implementation
L92@P1: of different repair strategies and how they might influence
L93@P1: users’ trust when a repeated failure takes place. We introduce
L94@P1: four different repair strategies: apology, apology with a
L95@P1: promise, apology with a warning and no apology. We hypothesise the following H2: The implementation of an apology
L96@P1: with a promise will lead to a more extensive decrease in
L97@P1: the users’ trust when a repeated failure is introduced, as
L98@P1: compared to other forms of repair strategies.
L99@P1: Additionally, we investigate what communication method
L100@P1: people follow when faced with an incongruence and forced
L101@P1: to pick between the two. We also investigate if there are
L102@P1: any individual differences (such as negative attitudes towards
L103@P1: robots or propensity to trust) among the participants, based
L104@P1: on whether they prefer verbal or non-verbal instructions, and
L105@P1: if they have any reasoning behind their preference.
L106@P1: II. RELATED WORK
L107@P1: Trust is stated to be an important aspect of any HRI
L108@P1: research when it comes to creating acceptance amongst
L109@P1: users, especially in scenarios of collaboration where it is
L110@P1: necessary that the users follow robot-produced suggestions
L111@P1: and decisions [10], [11]. A commonly used definition in
L112@P1: Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) focuses on human trust in
L113@P1: automation and can be defined as the attitude that: “an
L114@P1: agent will help achieve an individual’s goal in a situation
L115@P1: characterised by uncertainty and vulnerability” [12]. If the
L116@P1: robot’s behaviour deviates from the trusted behaviour, for
L117@P1: instance by committing a failure, this can impact the users’
L118@P1: trust [13].
L119@P1: A robot failure has been defined as: “a degraded state
L120@P1: of ability which causes the behaviour or service being
L121@P1: performed by the system to deviate from the ideal, normal
L122@P1: or correct functionality” [14]. Even though robot error is
L123@P1-2: generally regarded as a performance-based factor, the userFig. 1. Setup for block selection with Pepper. The colours of the blocks
L124@P2: vary between green, orange, blue and purple. The robot would always start
L125@P2: in the position shown in this figure, before moving towards one of the
L126@P2: blocks. When the robot moves it simultaneously gives the verbal indication
L127@P2: and the corresponding non-verbal gestures and the colour changed on the
L128@P2: tablet.
L129@P2: and their environment will also impact how the error is
L130@P2: interpreted and to what extent this impacts trust, for example
L131@P2: errors committed in stressful or novel environments [15].
L132@P2: Giuliani et al. [2] classified failures according to their type:
L133@P2: Technical failures - caused by technical shortcomings in
L134@P2: the robot and social norm violations - when the robot
L135@P2: deviates from the social script or uses inappropriate social
L136@P2: signals. A robot incongruence can often be perceived as
L137@P2: a social norm violation, although it might derive from a
L138@P2: technical shortcoming in the robot as well [2]. Previous
L139@P2: work has looked at robot incongruence in the form of facial
L140@P2: expressions [16], congruent and incongruent approach behaviour when giving different information [17], incongruent
L141@P2: robot gestures [9] and the use of different emotional cues
L142@P2: [18], [7]. While none of these studies looked specifically
L143@P2: at the relation between robot incongruence and users’ trust,
L144@P2: Tsiourti et al. [7] found that when an observer receives
L145@P2: incongruous emotional information across the auditory and
L146@P2: visual modalities, the incongruences confused their users and
L147@P2: impacted the robot’s likability and believability. Additionally,
L148@P2: Salem et al. [9] found that incongruence between the robot’s
L149@P2: gestures and what it said had a significant impact on users’
L150@P2: task performance, the perceived anthropomorphism of the
L151@P2: robot and the mental model users had of the robot’s abilities.
L152@P2: When robot failures take place, different forms of repair
L153@P2: strategies can be implemented to mitigate some of the
L154@P2: potential losses in trust [19]. As discussed by Esterwood and
L155@P2: Robert [19], the human-human literature has classified these
L156@P2: efforts as either apologies, denials, explanations, or promises.
L157@P2: The HRI literature on which is the best repair strategies is
L158@P2: rather mixed. At times. promises have been shown to be
L159@P2: a more effective repair strategy than general apologies or
L160@P2: denials [4], on the other hand explanations have been shown
L161@P2: to work better than apologies in certain instances, when
L162@P2: an apology is not necessarily warranted [20], [21]. Recent
L163@P2: work [22] found no real difference between repair strategies
L164@P2: (apology, explanation, promises), with only denials behaving
L165@P2: significantly worse.
L166@P2: Additionally, previous work has also looked at embellishing established repair strategies. For example, by having
L167@P2: the robot display remorse [23] while apologising, or by
L168@P2: acknowledging the mistake and handling it [21]. Though a lot
L169@P2: is currently undetermined in regards to HRI repair strategies,
L170@P2: there seems to be a general consensus on the efficacy of
L171@P2: apologies and acknowledging that mistakes have taken place.
L172@P2: We, therefore, design our repair strategies with this in mind,
L173@P2: creating a general apology as a baseline, and then adding
L174@P2: additional features in the form of a promise and a warning.
L175@P2: III. METHOD
L176@P2: In our video-based survey study, participants were tasked
L177@P2: with choosing between two blocks of different colours, based
L178@P2: on the robot’s verbal and non-verbal indications (see Figure
L179@P2: 1). This study was conducted online, via Microsoft Forms
L180@P2: Survey. Participants were recruited through Prolific1and
L181@P2: randomly allocated to one of four conditions, corresponding to the repair strategy the robot implemented after its
L182@P2: failure. Through Prolific, multiple screening criteria were
L183@P2: implemented to ensure that no vulnerable participants, or
L184@P2: those suffering from any form of colour vision impairment,
L185@P2: were invited to participate in the study.
L186@P2: Participants were debriefed and asked for consent before
L187@P2: they started the study. We gathered data on their age, gender,
L188@P2: propensity to trust robots [24] and their negative attitudes
L189@P2: towards robots [25]. They were then again debriefed on
L190@P2: the task they were to complete and asked to identify four
L191@P2: different colours. These colours were later used for the blocks
L192@P2: in the study. This test was included as an additional screening
L193@P2: process to limit the study’s exposure to people suffering
L194@P2: from colour blindness, beyond the preliminary screening
L195@P2: implemented in Prolific.
L196@P2: The main part of the study was divided into three different
L197@P2: parts, see Figure 2 for a flow diagram of the study. To ensure
L198@P2: that the failures had the same effect on all participants, the
L199@P2: ordering of these parts was kept the same. In all three parts,
L200@P2: participants are tasked with selecting a coloured block with
L201@P2: the help of a Pepper robot, see Figure 1. The blocks were
L202@P2: placed on a table and were either green, orange, blue or
L203@P2: purple. The robot indicated a block by saying the name of the
L204@P2: colour out-loud, while simultaneously indicating the block
L205@P2: by moving towards it, gesturing to it with both hands and a
L206@P2: head tilt, and changing the colour of its tablet to the same
L207@P2: colour as that of the block.
L208@P2: For the first part of the task, participants watched three
L209@P2: of these videos and selected a colour after each video. After
L210@P2: the third video, they were also asked to complete the Trust
L211@P2: in Automated Systems (TAS) scale [26], we will refer to
L212@P2: this measure as TAS1 throughout the rest of the paper. In
L213@P2: the first part, no robot failure is introduced, meaning that
L214@P2: there was no difference between what the robot said and
L215@P2: what it gestured towards. In the second part, participants
L216@P2: watched again three videos. However, in the third video of

L263@P3: To ensure that participants watched all the videos to the
L264@P3: end, multiple attention checks were set in place. After each

L269@P3: (TAS2) asking participants to select agree on a five-point

L272@P3: we added one manipulation check at the end of each part,

L385@P5: To investigate participants’ preferences further, we had a
L386@P5: closer look at the preliminary personal traits gathered: age,
L387@P5: gender, their propensity to trust robots and negative attitudes

L395@P5: participants who favoured voice had a significantly higher
